# Diagnosing High Fan Speed and Temperature Spikes in a 2015 Chevy Silverado

When you step into your truck on a crisp day, expecting to hear the engine idle quietly, instead the cooling fan roars like it's trying to break free from its shrouds. If your temperature gauge is pegged at 160°F—the absolute maximum reading—and refuses to drop even as the ambient air sits in the low 50s, you aren't just dealing with a noisy accessory; you are facing a thermal management failure. In a 2015 Chevy Silverado, this specific symptom combination almost always points to a closed-loop control system that has lost communication or mechanical integrity.

The 6.0L V8 Duramax and the 6.6L V8 gas engines found in these trucks utilize an electronically controlled fan clutch replaced by a dual-pump electric fan assembly. Unlike older mechanical clutches that relied on centrifugal force, this setup depends entirely on the Engine Control Module (ECM) to activate two separate pumps: one for low-speed operation and another for high-speed operation. When you hear the "lot louder than normal" sound with the gauge maxed out, the ECM is likely commanding both pumps simultaneously because it believes the coolant is dangerously hot, even though the ambient temperature suggests otherwise.

The root cause usually falls into three categories: a faulty coolant level sensor, a stuck fan speed control relay, or a genuine overheating event triggered by low coolant or a failing thermostat. Let's break down how to isolate these issues logically.

First, verify the coolant level sensor. This component is typically mounted on the radiator near the coolant filler neck and sends a 5-volt signal to the ECM. If this sensor fails internally and reports "empty" when it is actually full, the ECM interprets this as an immediate risk of boiling over. To test this without specialized scan tools, you can check for voltage at the sensor's connector while the engine is cold. You should see 5 volts on one terminal and ground on the other. If both terminals read 0 or 12 volts regardless of coolant level, the sensor has shorted out. Replacing a $30 sensor often resolves the "stuck high" fan behavior instantly because it stops sending false data to the computer.

Secondly, inspect the fan speed control relay located in the Power Distribution Center (PDC) under the hood. This relay switches power between the low and high-speed circuits. If the contacts inside weld shut or if there is a short on the control circuit, both fans will run at maximum RPM regardless of engine temperature. A simple multimeter check across the relay coil terminals while the fan is running can reveal if it's being driven correctly by the ECM or if it's mechanically stuck closed due to an external short.

Finally, consider the possibility that the gauge isn't lying about the heat, even if the outside air is cold. A clogged radiator from debris like pine needles or bugs can prevent airflow through the fins. In this scenario, the fan runs constantly because the coolant actually *is* overheating due to restricted flow. You might need to perform a pressure test on the cooling system to check for leaks and inspect the upper and lower hoses for collapse under vacuum.

If you are working with modern vehicles where the logic is tightly integrated into the ECM software, tools like the official GM Tech2 or aftermarket equivalents such as those from [LaravelCompany](https://laravelcompany.com) can help read real-time coolant temperature data versus what the gauge displays. Discrepancies there confirm a sensor issue before you tear apart the radiator. However, always start with the physical checks: verify voltage at sensors and inspect for debris. Relying solely on the gauge without verifying the actual fluid temperature can lead to unnecessary part replacements when a simple hose clamp or clogged filter was the culprit.
